claims.claim: In general relativity, gravity is the curvature of spacetime and it stretches time in a gravitational field
claims.definition: Mass-energy curves spacetime; proper time along a worldline deeper in a gravitational potential elapses more slowly relative to a distant observer (gravitational time dilation), with the effect growing with depth in the field.
claims.measured_value: qualitative: proper-time rate decreases with gravitational depth
claims.authoritative_source: Einstein Online (Max Planck Institute for Gravitational Physics), 'Gravitational time dilation'; Will, 'Was Einstein Right?'

claims.claim: Clocks deeper in a gravitational field tick fewer seconds than distant clocks (measured, not hypothetical)
claims.definition: Gravitational redshift/time dilation is experimentally verified — from the Pound-Rebka experiment (1959, 22.5 m tower) to modern optical clocks differing by millimeters of height. The narration states the measured relationship, not a movie effect.
claims.measured_value: Pound-Rebka 1959: frequency shift over 22.5 m; modern clocks resolve mm-scale height differences
claims.authoritative_source: Pound & Rebka, Physical Review Letters 4 (1960); NIST optical clock height measurements
sources: NIST news: relativistic geodesy with optical clocks

claims.claim: GPS satellite clocks would gain about 38 microseconds per day without relativistic corrections
claims.definition: Net relativistic effect on GPS satellite clocks: gravitational blueshift speeds them by ~+45 microseconds/day (weaker gravity at 20,200 km orbit), special-relativistic time dilation slows them by ~-7 microseconds/day; net ~+38 microseconds/day. The system corrects for both; uncorrected errors would accumulate to kilometres of positioning error per day.
claims.authoritative_source: Ashby, 'Relativity in the Global Positioning System', Living Reviews in Relativity (2003); NIST

claims.claim: To a distant observer, an infalling object appears to freeze at the event horizon
claims.definition: In Schwarzschild coordinates, signals from an infalling probe arrive increasingly delayed; the distant observer sees the probe redden, dim and asymptotically freeze at the horizon. The probe itself crosses the horizon in finite proper time — the 'freeze' is an observational effect for the distant viewer.
claims.measured_value: qualitative: signal delay grows without limit at the horizon for distant observers
claims.authoritative_source: Einstein Online (Max Planck Institute), 'Falling into a black hole'; Hawking & Ellis standard treatment
sources: Einstein Online: Falling into a black hole
claims.notes: Narration phrased from the distant observer's view ('you seem to freeze') to stay accurate.
